Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 76
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Cashier
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle, Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me, Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power

Vignette:
Aleksander Nowak is a 76-year-old widowed Polish-American man who works part-time as a cashier at a grocery store in a mid-sized Midwestern city. He came to the clinic after his adult daughter, alarmed by the deterioration she witnessed during a recent visit, made the appointment on his behalf and accompanied him to the first session. His PCL-5 score of 67 places him in the severe range, and the picture that emerged across the intake and early sessions was one of a man who had carried something enormous and largely alone for longer than he could account for.

Aleksander was a teenager living in a small city in Poland during a period of civil unrest and military escalation that turned his neighborhood into a contested zone almost without warning. He has described, in careful and halting English, a particular afternoon when he and his younger brother were crossing an open market square and artillery fire began without any prior sound or signal. The shells landed in sequence, each one closer than the last. His brother was struck by debris and went down. Aleksander pulled him behind a collapsed market stall and pressed himself flat against the rubble while the shelling continued around them. The smell of burning, the sound of other people screaming and then going silent, the sensation of the ground shaking beneath his chest — these were the textures of perhaps forty minutes that have never fully receded. His brother survived with permanent injuries. Aleksander emigrated in his twenties, married, raised children, and worked for decades in manufacturing. His wife died three years ago, and it was in the quiet that followed her death that the past seemed to return with new force.

He now describes his memories of that afternoon as coming to him primarily as images — the angle of smoke rising, the color of the stone dust, the particular way his brother's face looked when he turned it toward him. When these images arrive unbidden, Aleksander does not experience them as recollections. He has said that he is back there, that his hands tighten and his breathing changes and the grocery store around him disappears. At other times he can speak of the event with a flatness that surprises even him, as though he is recounting something that happened to someone else entirely, a detachment he finds neither comforting nor trustworthy.

What frightened him most in the present, he explained, was the sense that nowhere was genuinely safe. He had come to believe this not as an abstract proposition but as a practical fact that organized his daily life. At the grocery store where he works, he positions himself so that he can see the entrance at all times, and he watches customers as they approach his register, reading their faces and posture for any sign of threat. He has difficulty sleeping because lying still in the dark feels, in some part of him he cannot fully explain, like lowering his guard at the wrong moment. The world, he said quietly in the second session, had shown him what it was capable of, and he saw no reason to assume it had changed.

He stopped riding in cars shortly after his wife's death — the confinement, the speed, the inability to exit — and has arranged his life around walking distance. This has made his part-time cashier job, located twelve blocks from his apartment, the outer boundary of his world. He has declined family gatherings that require a drive, missed a grandchild's birthday, and watched the radius of his life contract without feeling he had any choice in the matter. He has also noticed that when something good happens — a kind word from a customer, an afternoon of autumn light — he pushes the feeling away before it can settle, as though allowing it would be a form of carelessness he could not afford.

He thinks often about why this happened to him, turning the question over without arriving anywhere. He no longer attends the church he went to with his wife for forty years. He has said, without bitterness but with great weariness, that he is no longer the man he understood himself to be — the one who worked hard, who endured, who provided. What brought him finally to the clinic was his daughter's face when she saw him: the fear in it, which he recognized.
